l: Eumolpus, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Eumolpus cleanses and initiates Hercules at Eleusis. He is the son of Poseidon by Chione, is thrown into the sea by his mother, rescued by Poseidon, and carried to Ethiopia. After being banished, he goes to Thrace, becomes its king, fights for the Eleusinians against the Athenians, and is killed by Erechtheus; he is the father of Ismarus.

l: Eurypylus, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Several figures named Eurypylus are recorded. Eurypylus son of Evaemon sues for Helen, leads the Ormenians against Troy, and is wounded there; Eurypylus son of Hercules by Eubote is also listed, as is Eurypylus son of Poseidon, king of Cos, who is slain by Hercules. Eurypylus son of Telephus fights for the Trojans and is slain by Neoptolemus, while Eurypylus son of Temenus hires men to murder his father.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Ulysses is told by Eumaeus to shoot the suitors and is accompanied by Eurylochus, who reports Circe's enchantments. He saves Glaucus son of Antenor with Menelaus, captures Helenus, learns from him how Ilium may be taken, recognizes Helen, helps steal the Palladium, speaks in the Wooden Horse, and is awarded Hecuba or Helenus.

l: Europa, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Europa is carried by Zeus in the form of a bull through the sea to Crete. She is described as the daughter of Agenor or Phoenix, bears Zeus Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys, is sought by her relatives, marries Asterius, gives a necklace to Harmonia, and has descendants recorded.

l: Zeus, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Zeus carries Europa to Crete in the form of a bull and fathers Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys by her. He is also recorded as the father of Hellen by Pyrrha or as Hellen's possible father, the father of the Graces, and the husband of Themis by whom the Fates are born. He sends a storm on the Greeks and later sends Harmonia and Cadmus to the Elysian Fields.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus, is born a seven-month child and reigns over Mycenae and Tiryns. He orders Hercules to perform his labours, refuses to recognize some of them, hides in a bronze jar under the earth, demands the surrender of Hercules' sons from Ceyx, wages war with the Athenians, and is killed; his sons are also slain.

l: Hector, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Hector is the firstborn son of Priam and Hecuba and marries Andromache. He kills Protesilaus, fights Ajax, sets fire to the Greek ships, is slain by Achilles, and has his body ransomed by Priam.

l: Priam, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Priam is the father of Hector, Hecuba's husband, and the father of Paris and other sons and daughters. After Hector's death, he ransoms Hector's body; after Alexander's death, Helen is assigned to Deiphobus.

l: Hecuba, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Hecuba is the daughter of Dymas and the second wife of Priam. She is the mother of Hector and Paris, has a dream, is awarded to Ulysses or Helenus after Troy, is turned into a bitch, and is buried in the Chersonnese.

l: Achilles, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Achilles slays Hector and later slays Memnon. His armour is made by Hephaestus, and Polyxena is sacrificed on his grave.

l: Helen, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Helen is described as the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis and as having been hatched from an egg. She is carried off by Theseus and later rescued by Pollux and Castor, marries Menelaus, and is carried off by Alexander from Sparta. The real Helen is taken by Hermes to Egypt while a phantom Helen goes to Troy; she later helps Ulysses steal the Palladium, is led away by Menelaus, and goes with him to the Elysian Fields.

l: Menelaus, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Menelaus marries Helen and later leads her away from Troy. He saves Glaucus with Ulysses, discovers the real Helen in Egypt, and goes with her to the Elysian Fields.

l: Hephaestus, The Library, Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by
s: Hephaestus is borne by Hera and is also described as a son of Zeus and Hera. He helps at Athena's birth, kills the giant Mimas, nails Prometheus to the Caucasus, gives weapons and objects to various figures, makes Harmonia's necklace and Achilles' armour, and dries up the river Scamander. He is also the father of Palaemon, Erichthonius, and Periphetes.

l: The Library, The Library, Hera, daughter of Cronus and
s: The unit concerns Hera, daughter of Cronus and Rhea, and records her conflicts, powers, cults, and actions involving gods and heroes. Hera persecutes Io, Hercules, Dionysus, Semele, Athamas, Ino, the Sphinx, Callisto, and others, while also aiding the Argonauts and being reconciled with Hercules. Zeus hangs Hera from Olympus, fears her, disputes with her before Tiresias, and makes Menelaus immortal. The Heraclids, the sons of Hercules, attack and conquer Peloponnese, later withdraw to Marathon, and seek to return.

l: Hera, The Library, Hera, daughter of Cronus and
s: Hera is the daughter of Cronus and Rhea; Cronus swallowed her, and she is the mother of Hephaestus. Zeus put her in bonds and hung her from Olympus, and he was afraid of her. She persecutes Io, Hercules, Dionysus, Semele, Athamas, Ino, and Callisto, sends the Sphinx to Thebes, and blinds Tiresias, but she also helps the Argonauts and is eventually reconciled with Hercules.

l: Zeus, The Library, Hera, daughter of Cronus and
s: Zeus puts Hera in bonds and hangs her from Olympus, while also being afraid of her. Zeus and Hera refer their dispute to Tiresias as arbiter; Zeus later makes Menelaus immortal.

l: Hercules, The Library, Hera, daughter of Cronus and
s: Hera sends serpents to kill the infant Hercules, drives him mad, stirs up the Amazons against him, afflicts the cows of Geryon with a gadfly, and sends storms against him. Hercules is eventually reconciled to Hera.

l: Heraclids, The Library, Hera, daughter of Cronus and
s: The Heraclids, the sons of Hercules, attack and conquer Peloponnese, then quit Peloponnese and retire to Marathon. Hyllus seeks to effect their return, Polyphontes is one of them, and they belong to the family of Inachus.

l: The Library, The Library, Herb, magical, which brings dead
s: This unit is an index of mythological figures, places, objects, and events, with extensive entries on Hercules and his labours, adventures, death, and descendants. It also records the deeds and relationships of Hermes, including his assistance to Hercules and Perseus. Zeus appears as a god involved in Hercules’s immortality, the golden apples, and various other myths. The unit includes entries for Eurystheus, who commands Hercules’s labours and receives the objects he retrieves.

l: Hercules, The Library, Herb, magical, which brings dead
s: Hercules performs numerous feats, including slaying Linus, the Nemean lion, the Lernaean hydra, Geryon, and other enemies; rescuing Alcestis and Prometheus; cleansing the cattle-yard of Augeas; retrieving the belt of Hippolyte, the golden apples of the Hesperides, and Cerberus; and capturing Troy, Elis, Pylus, and Lacedaemon. He serves Eurystheus at Tiryns, is named Alcides, marries Megara and later Hebe, fathers the Heraclids, and is eventually tortured by a poisoned robe before burning himself on Mount Oeta and obtaining immortality.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, Herb, magical, which brings dead
s: Eurystheus is served by Hercules at Tiryns after the Delphic oracle orders Hercules to undertake his labours. Hercules brings the Cerynitian hind, the Erymanthian boar, Hippolyte’s belt, Geryon’s kine, the golden apples of the Hesperides, and Cerberus to Eurystheus.

l: Zeus, The Library, Herb, magical, which brings dead
s: Zeus is associated with many events in the unit, including sending Hermes to Deucalion and ordering Hermes to steal Io in the form of a cow. He gives the winged horses to, and is connected with, several mythological figures; he receives sacrifices, grants Hercules immortality, and is involved in the myths of the Hesperides’ apples and the death of Iasion.

l: Hermes, The Library, Herb, magical, which brings dead
s: Hermes kills the giant Hippolytus and Argus the All-seeing, rescues Ares, guides Perseus to the Phorcides, gives Perseus an adamantine sickle, and gives Hercules a sword. He admonishes Hercules in Hades, sells Hercules to Omphale, gives moly to Ulysses, and serves as herald of the gods; he is also described as the son of Zeus and Maia, the father of several figures, and the maker of a lyre and a shepherd’s pipe.

l: The Library, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: The Isthmus of Corinth is associated with the Argo, the Cretan bull, Theseus, Sinis, an oracle, and the chariot race for Hippodamia's suitors. Italy is said to be named after a bull, and Greeks and Campanians settle there. Ulysses returns to Ithaca from Thesprotia, while Telegonus later comes to Ithaca. Ixion attempts to violate Hera, is deceived by a cloud resembling her, and is bound to a wheel.

l: the Isthmus of Corinth, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: The Argo is dedicated to Poseidon at the Isthmus of Corinth. The Cretan bull traverses it, Theseus clears it of malefactors, and Sinis is associated with it. It is also the subject of an oracle and is the goal of the chariot race for the suitors of Hippodamia.

l: Italy, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: Italy is said to be named after a bull. Greeks and Campanians settle in Italy, and Campania and the river Navaethus are mentioned there.

l: Penelope, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: Penelope's suitors include men from Ithaca.

l: Ithaca, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: Ulysses is in Ithaca and later returns there from Thesprotia. Ulysses is seen in sight of Ithaca, Penelope's suitors come from Ithaca, and Telegonus comes to Ithaca.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: Ulysses is in Ithaca and is later seen in sight of it. He returns to Ithaca from Thesprotia.

l: Ixion, The Library, Isthmian festival, the third, i. 249;
s: Ixion attempts to violate Hera and is deluded by a cloud in Hera's likeness. He is bound to a wheel and whirled through the air.

l: The Library, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: This unit is an index of mythological figures, places, objects, and events, including Jason’s quest for the Golden Fleece, Medea’s aid and later actions, and the roles of the Argo and Pelias. It also records numerous deeds of Hercules, Ulysses, Theseus, and Achilles. The entries describe battles, marriages, punishments, voyages, transformations, and deaths associated with these figures.

l: Jason, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the Calydonian boar, dwells in Iolcus, and is sent by Pelias to fetch the Golden Fleece. He is admiral of the Argo, wins the Golden Fleece with Medea’s help, flees with her, marries her in Corcyra, and later returns the fleece to Pelias. He is expelled from Iolcus with Medea, goes to Corinth, marries Glauce, divorces Medea, and helps Peleus lay waste to Iolcus.

l: Pelias, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Pelias sends Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece. When Jason returns to Iolcus, he receives the Golden Fleece from him; Medea later beguiles Pelias’s daughters into murdering their father.

l: Golden Fleece, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: The Golden Fleece is demanded by Jason from Aeetes. Jason wins it with Medea’s aid, flees with her, and later surrenders it to Pelias on returning to Iolcus.

l: Argo, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: The Argo is commanded by Jason, who serves as its admiral. Jason later dedicates the Argo to Poseidon at Corinth.

l: Medea, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Medea, daughter of Aeetes, is a witch who loves Jason and gives him a magic drug. She helps him procure the Golden Fleece, flees with him, murders her brother Apsyrtus, and marries Jason. After Jason divorces her, she burns Glauce, murders her own children, flees to Athens, marries Aegeus, plots against Theseus, and is expelled; she later returns to Colchis and restores her father’s kingdom.

l: Hercules, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Hercules completes ten labours in eight years and a month, including killing the Nemean lion, the Hydra, and the Cerynitian hind, driving away the cows of Geryon, and bringing the man-eating mares of Diomedes to Eurystheus. He fights the Lapiths, campaigns against Lacedaemon, kills Laomedon and Laogoras, and fights in many other places. His madness leads him to burn the children he had by Megara; he also buries Melas and throws Lichas into the sea.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Ulysses visits the Laestrygones and the Lotus-eaters, wanders through Libya, and is among the companions whose transformations are recorded. His comrades kill and eat the cows of the Sun. He pretends madness, scorns Melanthius, and kills him.

l: Theseus, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Theseus penetrates the Labyrinth with the help of a clue. He is sent against the bull of Marathon, carries off the Amazon Melanippe, and kills Lycomedes.

l: Achilles, The Library, Jason, son of Aeson, hunts the
s: Achilles is fed on the inwards of lions. He takes Lesbos, Lyrnessus, and Linaeum, captures Lycaon, and is recorded among the figures connected with the Trojan war.

l: The Library, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: This unit is an alphabetical index of mythological figures, places, and objects from Meleager through Olympus. It records genealogies, marriages, births, heroic deeds, wars, deaths, and transformations. It includes accounts of Meleager and the Calydonian boar, Menelaus and Helen’s movements after Troy, Minos and the Minotaur in the Labyrinth, and numerous exploits of Hercules. It also mentions the gods Zeus, Apollo, and Poseidon in connection with births, punishments, prophecies, and divine actions.

l: Meleager, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Meleager is described as the son of Oeneus or Ares and Althaea, with his life bound up with a burning brand. He hunts the Calydonian boar, kills the sons of Thestius, gives the boar’s skin to Atalanta, and later dies; he is also said to have been in the Argo and to have been seen by Hercules in Hades.

l: Hercules, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Hercules performs numerous labors and exploits in this unit, including killing the Nemean lion, fighting or killing monsters and enemies, capturing the Cretan bull, visiting Hades, and attacking Oechalia. He also participates in the Argonaut expedition, is initiated into the Mysteries of Eleusis, celebrates the Olympian games, and is burned on Mount Oeta.

l: Achilles, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Achilles slays Memnon at Troy.

l: Menelaus, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Menelaus, son of Atreus, becomes Helen’s husband and king of Sparta. He helps Agamemnon, goes to Troy with Ulysses to demand Helen’s restoration, fights Alexander, slays Deiphobus, and leads Helen away; after wandering through several lands, he finds Helen in Egypt, returns to Sparta, and goes with her to the Elysian Fields.

l: Helen, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Helen is chosen as Menelaus’s wife and is taken away by Alexander. Menelaus later finds her in Egypt, returns with her to Sparta, and goes with her to the Elysian Fields.

l: Agamemnon, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Agamemnon is helped by Menelaus to expel Thyestes and later leads the Mycenaeans against Troy. Menelaus asks him to muster an army against Troy, and Agamemnon and Cassandra are later murdered at Mycenae.

l: Troy, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Troy is attacked by the Greeks, against whom Memnon brings a force of Ethiopians. The city is later sacked, and several events involving the Trojan war and its aftermath are recorded.

l: Greeks, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: The Greeks send Menelaus and Ulysses to Troy to demand the restoration of Helen and muster forces against Troy. After the sack of Ilium, some of them sail to Mimas, while Nauplius later lures others onto the breakers with false lights.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Ulysses goes with Menelaus to Troy to demand the restoration of Helen and later fetches Neoptolemus from Scyros. He wanders through the Ocean and various places, uses Moly as an antidote to Circe’s enchantments, deceives Polyphemus by calling himself Nobody, and is later condemned to exile by Neoptolemus.

l: Apollo, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Apollo, with Artemis, shoots down the children of Niobe. He is also named as the father of Miletus and Mopsus.

l: Minos, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Minos becomes king of Crete, passes laws, marries Pasiphae, and has several children, including Androgeus and Ariadne. He receives Talos from Hephaestus, fails to sacrifice a bull to Poseidon, shuts the Minotaur in the Labyrinth, and uses Polyidus to recover Glaucus from the dead; he later attacks Athens, captures Megara, and is undone by the daughters of Cocalus.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Poseidon is the father of Neleus, Nauplius, and others named in the unit. He gives Minos the bull connected with Minos’s vow, breaks off part of Cos to form Nisyrum, hides Oenopion from Orion in an underground house, and is associated with the sea and several divine transformations.

l: Minotaur, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: The Minotaur is a bull-headed man, offspring of Pasiphae and a bull. Minos confines it in the Labyrinth, and Theseus is sent against it and kills it.

l: Labyrinth, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: The Labyrinth is the place where Minos confines the Minotaur. Minos also shuts Daedalus in it before pursuing him to Sicily.

l: Zeus, The Library, Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares
s: Zeus is the father of the Muses by Mnemosyne and of several other figures named in the unit. He swallows Metis after learning of a prophecy concerning her son, hangs Hera from Olympus, turns nymphs into the Hyades, and has encounters with Nemesis in different forms.

l: The Library, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: This unit records mythological figures and places from Omphale through Phineus, including their genealogies, deeds, journeys, deaths, and cults. It gives extensive accounts of Hercules, Pelops, Perseus, Peleus, Orestes, and others, as well as events involving the Trojan War and the Argonauts. It also describes oracles, sacred objects such as the Palladium, and the origins of cities, peoples, festivals, and sanctuaries.

l: Hercules, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Hercules was bought as a slave by Omphale, queen of Lydia, and served her. He fought Amyntor at Ormenium, attacked the sons of Minos at Paros, diverted the Peneus into the cattle-yard of Augeas, founded an altar to Pelops at Olympia, and was the father of several sons, including Onesippus, Onites, Patroclus, Palaemon, and others.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Poseidon fathered or was associated with numerous figures, including Orion, Pelias, Otus and Ephialtes, Periclymenus, and Pegasus. He received Pelops’ prayer, gave Pelops a winged chariot, fortified Pergamum with Apollo, and later turned the ship of the Phaeacians to stone.

l: Peloponnese, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: The Peloponnese was formerly called Apia and was inhabited by Pelasgians. It was conquered by the Heraclids, who were first defeated and later finally conquered it; it was also associated with the rule of Tisamenus and with the exile of Laius.

l: Patroclus, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Patroclus, son of Hercules by Pyrippe, is listed among the children of Hercules. Patroclus, son of Menoetius, was a suitor of Helen, killed Clitonymus, took refuge with Peleus, accompanied Achilles to Troy, and was killed by Hector; games were held in his honour.

l: Oracle at Delphi, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: The Oracle at Delphi gave commands and predictions concerning Athamas, Pelias, Jason and the Argo, Hercules, the Heraclids, Thebes, Alcmaeon, Ilium, Aeacus, Oenomaus, Thyestes, Orestes, and the image of Tauropolus. It also declared that the Mycenaeans should choose a Pelopid as king and that Ilium required the propitiation of Athena.

l: Delphi, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Delphi was the site of the oracle that gave guidance on many mythological events. Orestes was tried there after killing Neoptolemus, and he later slew Neoptolemus at Delphi.

l: Jason, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Jason was sent by Pelias to fetch the Golden Fleece. The Oracle at Delphi also gave an oracle concerning the Argo.

l: Argo, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: The Argo carried Jason and the Argonauts, including Hercules, Orpheus, Peleus, Periclymenus, Phanus, and Palaemon. It reached the river Phasis in Colchis, and Phineus revealed the course of its voyage.

l: Heraclids, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: The Heraclids conquered the Peloponnese, were defeated by the Peloponnesians, and later returned and conquered it finally. Oxylus served as their guide, while Pamphylus was their ally and was killed in battle.

l: Ilium, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Ilium was associated with the Palladium, which had to remain within the city for Troy not to be taken. An oracle concerned the foundation of Ilium, Athena was to be propitiated there, and the bones of Pelops were required for its capture.

l: Athena, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Athena flayed the giant Pallas and used his skin as a shield. She received the Gorgon’s head from Perseus, and she gave Pandrosus Erichthonius in a chest; her Palladium was the image of Pallas, daughter of Triton.

l: Penelope, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Penelope was the wife of Ulysses and mother of Telemachus. She deceived her suitors by undoing her web, gave them Ulysses’ bow, and was said either to have borne Poliporthes to Ulysses or to have borne Pan to Hermes; another account says Telegonus conveyed her to Circe, after which she married Telegonus.

l: Orpheus, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Orpheus attempted to bring his dead wife Eurydice back from Hades and was known for his music. He was said to have invented the mysteries of Dionysus, was torn apart by the Maenads, joined the Argo, and restrained the Argonauts from the Sirens.

l: Apollo, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Apollo served Admetus as a herdsman at Pherae. Together with Poseidon, he fortified Pergamum, and Philoctetes founded a sanctuary dedicated to Apollo the Wanderer and dedicated his bow there.

l: Dionysus, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Dionysus was associated with the mysteries attributed to Orpheus. His son Peparethus was born to Ariadne.

l: Ares, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Ares fathered Penthesilea by Otrere and was associated with several genealogies, including Cycnus and Pelopia. Otus and Ephialtes, sons of Poseidon, put Ares in bonds.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Ulysses detected Palamedes’ feigned madness and later caused Palamedes to be stoned as a traitor at Troy. He stole the Palladium from Troy, helped fetch Philoctetes, returned to Ithaca, and with Philoetius helped shoot the suitors; he was the husband of Penelope.

l: Palladium, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: The Palladium was granted by Zeus to Ilus, and its origin was connected with Pallas, daughter of Triton. Troy was not to be taken while it remained within the walls, but Ulysses stole it.

l: Zeus, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Zeus was the father of Order and Peace by Themis, of Pan by Hybris, and of Persephone by Styx. He also fathered Perseus by Danae and granted the Palladium to Ilus.

l: Paris, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Paris, the second son of Priam and Hecuba, was exposed on Mount Ida, suckled by a bear, and later called Alexander. He carried a phantom of Helen to Troy, and Phereclus built his ships.

l: Peleus, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Peleus was the son of Aeacus and Endeis, joined the Argonauts, hunted the Calydonian boar, and wrestled with Atalanta. He accidentally killed Eurytion, married Thetis, fathered Achilles, brought Achilles to Chiron, and was later expelled from Phthia by the sons of Acastus.

l: Thetis, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Thetis married Peleus on Mount Pelion and was the mother of Achilles. Peleus prevented her from making Achilles immortal.

l: Achilles, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Achilles was the son of Peleus and Thetis and was taken to Chiron by Peleus. He killed Penthesilea, sent Patroclus to fight the Trojans, and was buried with Patroclus in the White Isle.

l: Medea, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Medea instigated the murder of Pelias by his daughters. She also killed Perses after he deposed Aeetes.

l: Philoctetes, The Library, Omphale, mistress of Hercules,
s: Philoctetes was the son of Poeas and a suitor of Helen. After being bitten by a snake at Tenedos, he was abandoned by the Greeks in Lemnos, later fetched by Ulysses and Diomedes, and used his bow to shoot Alexander; he settled at Crimissa and founded a sanctuary of Apollo the Wanderer.

l: The Library, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: The unit records mythological figures, places, and events from Phlegra through Python and the Quail. It describes Hercules's battles, labors, and encounters, including his role at Phlegra and his connection with the Pillars of Hercules. It also covers Trojan-war figures and events, including Achilles's capture of Phocaea, Ulysses's actions, Priam's history, and Agamemnon's role. Several entries concern Apollo, Persephone, Hades, and related divine or heroic episodes.

l: Hercules, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Hercules is said to have fought in the battle of the gods with the giants at Phlegra. The Pillars of Hercules are mentioned, and Hercules is associated with numerous entries throughout the unit, including the capture of Cerberus, the rescue of Theseus but not Pirithous from Hades, and the burial of Pholus.

l: Achilles, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Achilles took Phocaea. The unit also mentions the grave of Achilles, at which Polyxena was slaughtered by the Greeks.

l: Troy, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Troy is the destination of the Phocians, Phrygians, and other forces in the Trojan war. The unit records that the Locrians ceased to send suppliants to Troy after the Phocian war and that the Wooden Horse was stationed at Priam's palace.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Ulysses took a Phrygian prisoner and later blinded Polyphemus by making him drunk. Poseidon became angry with Ulysses, broke up his raft, and caused the Phaeacians' ship to turn to stone before being propitiated by Ulysses.

l: Apollo, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Apollo is associated with the theft of his kine by Hermes in Pieria. He also killed Python, the snake guarding the oracle at Delphi, and granted Cassandra the art of prophecy.

l: Persephone, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Persephone was carried off by Pluto, who gave her a pomegranate seed to eat. She was sent up from the underworld, while Pirithous tried to win her as a wife and was detained in Hades.

l: Hades, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Hades is identified as the abode ruled by Pluto. Hercules saw Pirithous in Hades but failed to rescue him, while Theseus was also detained there.

l: Agamemnon, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Agamemnon and Menelaus were brought to Polybus by their nurse. Agamemnon is also listed among the figures connected with the Trojan war.

l: Priam, The Library, Phlegra, Hercules in the battle of
s: Priam was formerly called Podarces and was the son of Laomedon. Hercules spared him, and Hesione redeemed him; later he became king of Ilium, ransomed Hector's body, and was slain by Neoptolemus.

l: The Library, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: This unit is an index of mythological figures, places, objects, and events from the stories of the gods, heroes, and the Trojan War. It records accounts involving Zeus, Hera, Hercules, Dionysus, Medea, Theseus, Ulysses, Achilles, and Poseidon, along with events at Troy and Ilium and in Hades. It also lists genealogies, transformations, sacrifices, deaths, resurrections, journeys, and punishments.

l: Zeus, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Zeus receives the sacrifice of the golden-fleeced ram, is the father of Rhadamanthys by Europa, and is the father of Sarpedon by Europa or Laodamia. He fathers the Seasons by Themis and Taygete's son Lacedaemon, ordains oaths by the water of Styx, and is involved in the births of Dionysus and Persephone.

l: Hercules, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Hercules effects the resurrection of Alcestis, receives the poisoned robe from Athena, kills the Scironian and Stymphalian foes, and serves Admetus, Eurystheus, and Omphale under different conditions. He captures Ilium with Telamon, gives Sterope a lock of the Gorgon's hair, heals or guides various heroes, and performs many labours including shooting the Stymphalian birds and crossing the sea in the Sun's golden goblet.

l: Dionysus, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Dionysus brings Semele up from Hades, gives her the name Thyone, and ascends with her to heaven. He is purified and taught rites of initiation by Rhea, and his attendants, the Satyrs, are captured by Lycurgus and later released.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Ulysses helps Diomedes kill Rhesus, sails past Scylla and the Sirens, sacrifices to the souls of the dead, and helps capture Troy. He shoots the suitors of Penelope with Telemachus, is killed by Telegonus with a sting-ray spine, and is later carried to Circe.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Poseidon fathers Rhode by Amphitrite, Salamis by an unnamed mother in the entry, and Sarpedon in one genealogy. He fathers the river Scamander's lineage, gives birth to or is named as the father of several heroes, and turns the ship of the Phaeacians to stone.

l: Medea, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Medea gives Glauce a robe steeped in poison and kills Talos, the brazen guardian of Crete. The Sun gives her a dragon-car, and she is associated with the discovery of Talos's vulnerability.

l: Ilium, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Ilium is sacked by the Greeks. Hercules and Telamon previously capture the city, and the Greeks later destroy it after the Trojan War.

l: Theseus, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Theseus kills Sciron, Sinis, and the Crommyonian sow, and he takes Helen away with Pirithous. He is identified by the sword and sandals that serve as tokens of Aegeus's fatherhood.

l: Hera, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Hera is the wife of Zeus and receives the golden apple as an object of contention with Athena and Aphrodite. She sends the Sphinx to Thebes, sends serpents against the infant Hercules, casts Side into Hades, and is associated with the death or punishment of several figures.

l: Helen, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Helen is the object of the suit of many Greek heroes. She is carried off from Sparta by Alexander, and she had earlier been carried off by Theseus and Pirithous.

l: Menelaus, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Menelaus is summoned to Sparta by Tyndareus, reigns there with Helen, and returns to Sparta after the Trojan War. He is listed among the figures connected with the suitors of Helen and with the Greek expedition against Troy.

l: Troy, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Troy is attacked during the Trojan War, which lasts ten years, and is eventually sacked by the Greeks. The Scaean Gate, Ilium, and several Greek and Trojan heroes are associated with the city's capture.

l: Achilles, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Achilles shoots at the Scaean Gate, takes the cities of Side and Smyrna, and wounds Telephus. He heals Telephus with rust from his spear and kills Tenes at Tenedos.

l: Hades, The Library, Ram with golden fleece carries
s: Hades contains the punishments of Sisyphus and Tantalus and the stone of Ascalaphus. Alcestis, Semele, and other figures are brought back from Hades, while the souls of the dead flee at the sight of Hercules and are seen by Ulysses.

l: The Library, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: This unit is an alphabetical index covering mythological figures, places, events, and objects from Tereis through Urania. It records genealogies, marriages, transformations, heroic deeds, wars, deaths, and journeys, especially those involving Theseus, Tiresias, Troy, the Trojan war, and Ulysses. It also summarizes the histories of Thebes, the Thebans, Hercules, Dionysus, Poseidon, Thetis, Achilles, and related figures.

l: Penelope, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Penelope is identified as the wife whom Ulysses woos, and many suitors are listed as seeking her hand. Ulysses later returns to her, makes himself known to her, and kills the suitors.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Poseidon fathers or is associated with numerous figures, including Thasus, Triton, Polyphemus, and Theseus. He floods the Thriasian plain, sends the Marathonian bull, and is propitiated by Ulysses.

l: Thebans, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: The Thebans expose one of their sons each month to the Teumessian vixen, pay tribute to Erginus, and later resist the Argives. They seek Tiresias's counsel, abandon Thebes after defeat, and found Hestiaea.

l: Hercules, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Hercules conquers or attacks numerous places and peoples, including Thasos, the Thracians, the Thesprotians, and the Amazons. He also rescues Hesione, fights at Themiscyra, takes the tripod from Delphi, and is associated with many children by different women.

l: Dionysus, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Dionysus proves to the Thebans that he is a god, drives the women of Thebes mad, and traverses Thrace. He also turns pirates into dolphins, takes refuge with Thetis, and gives his mother Semele the name Thyone after raising her from the dead.

l: Tiresias, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Tiresias is a blind Theban soothsayer, the son of Everes and Chariclo, whose sight is lost and whose sex changes repeatedly. He advises the Thebans to sacrifice a human being and later to abandon the city; Ulysses consults his ghost, and he directs Ulysses to propitiate Poseidon.

l: Thebes, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Thebes is founded by Cadmus and later ruled by Polydorus, Lycus, and Creon. It is afflicted by the Sphinx, receives Oedipus, becomes the scene of the war of the Seven Champions, and is eventually captured by the Athenians and the Epigoni before being abandoned and taken by the Argives.

l: Oedipus, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Oedipus arrives in Thebes, where the city is afflicted by the Sphinx. He is later expelled from Thebes, and Theseus receives him among the Athenians.

l: Theseus, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Theseus clears the road from Troezen to Athens, kills several evildoers, defeats the Minotaur, and succeeds to the sovereignty of Athens. He fights with Hercules against the Amazons, marries Phaedra, fathers Acamas and Demophon, receives Oedipus, captures Thebes with the Athenians, carries off Helen, and is eventually killed by Lycomedes.

l: Diomedes, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Diomedes is the son of Tydeus and participates in the Trojan war. He accompanies Ulysses in killing Dolon and Rhesus, goes with him to Lemnos to fetch Philoctetes, and helps steal the Palladium from Troy.

l: Thetis, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Thetis is a Nereid who saves Hephaestus and helps guide the Argo through the Wandering Rocks. She is the daughter of Nereus, marries Peleus after changing shape to escape him, and is the mother of Achilles; she also advises and protects Achilles and Neoptolemus.

l: Achilles, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Achilles is the son of Peleus and Thetis and is essential to the capture of Troy. He fights at Troy, kills Troilus and Thersites, is warned by Thetis about Tenes and the first landing at Troy, and has his arms awarded to Ulysses after his death.

l: Troy, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Troy is named after Tros and is besieged during the Trojan war. It cannot be taken without Achilles, the bow of Hercules, and the removal of the Palladium; the Greeks eventually lay it waste.

l: Trojans, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: The Trojans refuse to restore Helen and are joined by allies during the siege. They chase the Greeks within their walls, later flee before Patroclus and Achilles, bring the Wooden Horse into Troy, and are slain by the Greeks.

l: Trojan War, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: The Trojan war includes the muster of the Greek army, the Greek expedition against Troy, and the ten-year siege. Telephus shows the Greeks the way, Philoctetes brings the bow of Hercules, and the war ends after the Wooden Horse and the fall of Troy.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: Ulysses is the son of Laertes and Anticleia, the husband of Penelope, and the leader of the Cephallenians against Troy. He helps organize the Greek campaign, kills Dolon and Rhesus with Diomedes, wins Achilles' arms, steals the Palladium, invents and enters the Wooden Horse, survives a long return journey, and is eventually killed unwittingly by his son Telegonus.

l: Wooden Horse, The Library, Tereis, mother of Megapenthes by
s: The Wooden Horse is invented by Ulysses and entered by him and fifty others. The Trojans drag it into Troy, after which the Greeks emerge and destroy the city.

l: The Library, The Library, Vine discovered by Dionysus,
s: The unit is an index of mythological entries from Vine through Zeuxippe. It records Dionysus’s association with the vine, wine, Icarius, Oeneus, and Lycurgus. It gives an extensive account of Zeus, including his ancestry, offspring, punishments, transformations, and interventions in the stories of gods and heroes. It also records episodes involving Hercules, Hera, and Athena, along with entries for many other figures and objects.

l: Dionysus, The Library, Vine discovered by Dionysus,
s: Dionysus discovered the vine and gave the vine-plant to Oeneus. He taught Icarius wine-brewing and gave him a branch of the vine; he drove Lycurgus mad, causing Lycurgus to mistake his son for a branch. Zeus entrusted Dionysus to Hermes, changed him into a kid, and later gave birth to him after carrying him in his thigh.

l: Hercules, The Library, Vine discovered by Dionysus,
s: Hercules sacrificed to Zeus Saviour and was rescued by Zeus when wounded. He killed or was involved in the deaths of various figures and monsters, including the vixen and dog in one account, and Zeus parted him from Apollo.

l: Zeus, The Library, Vine discovered by Dionysus,
s: Zeus was the son of Cronus and Rhea, ruler of the sky, husband of Hera, and father of numerous gods and heroes. He fought the Titans, Typhon, and the giants; ordained oaths by the water of Styx; punished or transformed many figures; and caused or ended several major events, including the great flood. He fathered or encountered figures including Athena, Dionysus, Hercules, Perseus, Helen, Castor, Pollux, Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, Amphion, and Zethus, and intervened repeatedly in the affairs of gods, heroes, and cities.

l: Hera, The Library, Vine discovered by Dionysus,
s: Hera married Zeus and was the mother or associate of several divine offspring. Zeus hung her from Olympus, inspired Porphyrion with lust for her, and later placed a cloud in her likeness beside Ixion. She and Zeus referred their dispute about the relative pleasure of men and women to Tiresias.

l: Athena, The Library, Vine discovered by Dionysus,
s: Athena was born from Zeus’s head after Zeus swallowed the pregnant Metis. Zeus and Athena were ordered to purify the Danaids, and Zeus and Poseidon appointed arbiters in the dispute between Athena and Poseidon over possession of Attica. Zeus also interposed the aegis between Athena and Pallas.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: This document is Henry T. Riley’s literal English translation of Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Books I–VII, supplied with an introduction, extensive notes, a synoptical view, and later transcriber, publication, and Project Gutenberg licensing material. The introduction presents Ovid’s life, poetic career, exile to Tomi, death, and major works, while the notes repeatedly explain names, variant traditions, allegories, historical rationalizations, and comparisons with Scripture. The poem begins with its stated purpose: to tell of forms changed into new bodies from the creation of the world to Augustus’s time. Book I orders Chaos into the cosmos, creates man, traces humanity’s decline through the four ages, and brings Jupiter’s flood after Lycaon’s impiety. Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulate the earth from stones. Subsequent transformations include Python’s death, Daphne becoming a laurel, Io’s suffering and restoration, Argus’s eyes becoming the peacock’s ornaments, and Phaëton’s journey toward the Sun. Books II–III continue with Phaëton’s fatal chariot ride, Calisto, Coronis, Ocyrrhoe, Battus, Aglauros, Europa, and Cadmus’s founding of Thebes. They also center on the harsh consequences of divine desire, pride, prophecy, and resistance: Actæon is changed into a stag; Semele dies in Jupiter’s splendor while Bacchus is saved; Narcissus becomes a flower; and Pentheus is destroyed for opposing Bacchus. Books IV–VI frame many tales within storytellers and contests. They include Pyramus and Thisbe, Venus and Mars, Salmacis and Hermaphroditus, the daughters of Minyas, Ino and Cadmus, Perseus and Andromeda, Proserpina’s abduction and Ceres’s search, Arachne’s weaving contest with Minerva, Niobe’s loss of her children, Latona’s Lycians becoming frogs, and the revenge of Progne and Philomela against Tereus. Book VII turns chiefly to Jason and Medea. Medea enables Jason to win the Golden Fleece, rejuvenates Æson, destroys Pelias, and, abandoned by Jason, kills Creon, Jason’s new bride, and her own children before escaping. The book then follows Medea’s failed attempt to poison Theseus, Minos’s threatened war against Athens, Æacus’s plague-stricken kingdom and the creation of the Myrmidons from ants, and Cephalus’s account of jealousy and the accidental death of Procris. The document ends with editorial and licensing records.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: An electronic, grave and dignified compendium of mythological narratives of ancient Greece and Rome, translated literally by Henry T. Riley with notes and explanations. It begins by declaring a design to speak of forms changed into new bodies, then unfolds through Books I-VII as principal transformations and variations of bodies.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ovid is a Roman poet, born in Sulmo in 43 B.C. Educated in Rome under distinguished masters, he completed his studies through visits to Athens and Asia Minor and lived in Sicily for nearly a year. At his father’s urging he briefly practiced law and held minor state offices after attaining his majority, but abandoned the law courts for poetry. He became intimate with distinguished poets and, as a favored poet, received royal-family patronage. His first youthful marriage was unhappy, his second brief, and his third lasting and devoted. He was prosperous and happy until about age fifty. Around 8 A.D. Augustus banished him from Rome to Tomi, where he died in 18 A.D. while still in banishment. He wrote poetry including the Amores, Heroic Epistles, Ars Amatoria, Remedia Amoris, Metamorphoses, Fasti, Tristia, Epistles, and minor poems. Metamorphoses, in fifteen books, is identified as his masterpiece and as a work checked against a Latin original. In its narratives he follows prevailing tradition in presenting a divine decision, deliberated by Jupiter and the Gods, to punish wicked mankind by a deluge. He gives Deucalion the merit belonging to Noah, treats the flood as universal though it was generally said to affect Thessaly only, and includes anachronisms involving the Molossi and frankincense. He alone names Pyreneus, is the earliest writer noted for the Pierides’ challenge to the Muses, and uses Arachne’s contest with Minerva to introduce further myths, including the Pygmies’ warfare with the Cranes.

s: summarizes The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII [Books I-VII] This section gives a book-by-book summary of the principal transformations in Books I-VII. It describes events from the division of Chaos through the stories of Jason, Medea, Ægeus, Theseus, and Minos.
