s: is_a portion of Ovid’s Metamorphoses [covered by the e-text] These books cover transformations and mythological narratives involving the creation of the world, the Ages of man, the Deluge, gods and heroes, and the adventures of Jason and Medea.

l: Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Greece, frequently called Achaia, receives the worship of Isis when Inachus settles there; Isis is later identified with Io. During Erectheus’s reign, famine leads Greece to seek corn from Egypt, while Ceres’s search for Proserpine helps establish or spread agricultural worship and mysteries; improved tilling may likewise come from Egypt. Greece is portrayed as transmitting luxurious manners through colonists and supplies noble youths for Jason’s expedition to recover Athamas’s treasures and avenge Phryxus.

l: Rome, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: worships Ino [under the name Matuta] Rome was where Ovid was brought for education and where he spent much of his early career in the forum. He later left Rome under Augustus’s edict and never returned.

l: Greek and Roman mythology, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Greek and Roman mythology is presented as a compendium of antiquity’s learning, traditions, manners, and customs, and as the subject of Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Books I–VII. Its narratives may embellish Phoenician or Egyptian origins, as with Io, and include Europa’s famous abduction.

l: Ovid’s Metamorphosis, translated grammatically, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ovid’s Metamorphosis is Henry Thomas Riley’s translation, originally published in 1851 in Bohn’s Classical Library. This e-text covers Books I–VII, uses the David McKay edition, and is checked against the George Bell edition and, where appropriate, Latin originals. Throughout, it records numerous textual variations and line-number errors.

l: Apollodorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Apollodorus is a person whose records mention Cycnus and Tiresias’s mother, place Ericthonius’s birth in Attica, preserve Europa’s genealogy, rank Semele as Thyone, reverse Philomela, Progne, and Tereus’s transformations, and recount Proserpine’s stays and Ascalaphus’s punishment and change into an owl.

l: Pausanias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pausanias is an ancient author who writes Arcadica, Attica, Laconica, Corinthiaca, and Bœotica. Across these works he records traditions, places, tombs, deluges, and accounts of figures including Lycaons, Cecrops’s daughters, Pentheus, Tereus, Orithyïa, Alpheus, Arethusa, and Narcissus. He weighs such stories critically: supporting some historical bases, accepting Alpheus’s course because of an oracle, and treating the passions of Alpheus and Narcissus’s transformation as fables or fiction.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: God is a deity, architect, Contriver, and Creator associated with ordering and forming the universe. With Nature, God ends Chaos’s primordial discord by dividing it into four Elements, separating earth, sea, heaven, and atmosphere, assigning proper places and inhabitants, and bringing the elements into harmonious regularity. God shapes the world and its sea, rivers, landforms, climates, air, winds, stars, and living creatures, commands plains with ease and infinite power, and forms man from earth, water, and divine elements, giving man an upward-looking countenance and dominion. Some ancient philosophers describe God not as creator but as organizer of pre-existent matter. Seeing mankind’s great wickedness, God resolves to punish earth and destroy mankind and other living creatures by a deluge, while promising that Deucalion’s deluge will be the last.

l: Chaos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Chaos is the original state of the universe: pre-existent matter, a rude and undigested mass in which sea, earth, heaven, stars, and discordant atoms are heaped together without form or order. At the beginning of nature, God, the Deity, and bounteous Nature end its discord by separating, arranging, and dividing it into four Elements, from which the ordered world is formed.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter is a God, king of heaven, omnipotent Father, ruler of the world and Gods, and possessor of heaven, the sceptre, thunder, and lightning. Son of Saturn and brother of Neptune and Pluto, he rules after Saturn is driven into Tartarus, shortens perpetual spring, and divides the year into four periods. When Giants seek heaven, he fights them with lightning, breaks their mountain structure, and buries them beneath mountains. Confronting human corruption, he visits Lycaon, punishes him by turning him into a wolf and burning his house, then resolves on a universal deluge. He sends rain rather than thunder, but afterward spares the guiltless Deucalion and Pyrrha and clears the sky. His later actions combine judgment, power, and repeated disguises or sexual pursuits: he changes Io into a heifer, has Epaphus by her, and has Argus killed; he strikes Phaëton with lightning to restrain world-threatening flames; he deceives and assaults Calisto in Diana's form and fathers Arcas; and, as a bull, carries Europa to Crete. He is also father of Mercury, Perseus, Bacchus, Æacus, and others named in the records. He approaches Semele with moderated thunder but still burns her, grants Tiresias prophetic knowledge, and mediates between Ceres and Pluto over Proserpine, dividing the year between them. Near the end, he answers Æacus with lightning and thunder and changes ants into men to supply Æacus with a new people. The records also say several persons may have borne his name, making some adventures uncertainly assigned.

l: Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Giants are a group that attempts to dispossess Jupiter and conquer Heaven. Aspiring to rule there, they heap Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa into a mountain structure to reach the stars. Jupiter strikes them with lightning, and they are buried beneath the mountains they piled.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Deucalion is a man, son of Prometheus, king of Thessaly, and husband of Pyrrha. Amid universal corruption, he is credited as at least one just man: the most upright among men and their greatest lover of justice. Saved with Pyrrha for virtuous conduct, he survives the Deluge, described as the only man surviving it, reaching Mount Parnassus in a little ship; records also say he flees there with some subjects. When the waters recede, he mourns the empty world and, with Pyrrha, seeks guidance to repair the loss of their race. He interprets Themis's response as an instruction to throw stones behind them, helping renew the human race. Afterward he raises an altar to Jupiter the Liberator, goes to Athens, builds a temple to Jupiter, and institutes sacrifices in Jupiter's honor. He lives before worship of Apollo at Delphi, becomes ancestor of Athamas, and after death receives a temple and worship as a divinity.

l: Pyrrha, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pyrrha, a woman descended from the Titans, is Epimetheus’s daughter and Deucalion’s wife. More regardful of the deities than any other woman, she survives the Deluge with Deucalion and reaches Parnassus as its only saved woman. They pray, grieve as the apparent sole survivors, and receive a response. Pyrrha first refuses to cast what she believes are her mother’s bones, but, after Deucalion explains, she throws stones behind her. Her stones renew the female race, helping restore humankind.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Deucalion's deluge is a universal punishment and destruction sent by Jupiter because of universal corruption, intended to destroy the mortal race and the world. Jupiter calls the council of the Gods and determines that mankind must be destroyed. The deluge then covers the land, erases the distinction between sea and land, and carries away crops, groves, animals, people, houses, and temples. It overflows Thessaly, transforms Phocis into sea and a wide plain of waters, and destroys men and animals. Deucalion and Pyrrha alone survive, as the only saved persons. It is described as the last deluge.

l: Python, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Python is an enormous, unheard-of serpent produced by the Earth, occupying much of a mountain and terrifying the new race of men. Apollo slays it with a thousand arrows. Philosophically it represents reptiles born from flood slime and destroyed by the sun’s heat; historically, it may represent a robber near Parnassus.

l: Phœbus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phœbus, also called Apollo and Hyperion, is a god: the bow-bearing, Delian son of Latona, twin brother of Diana, and a luminous heavenly body or sun whose chariot carries light to the universe. At the beginning, he kills the serpent Python with arrows, then takes the surname Pythius and establishes the Pythian games to preserve the deed’s fame. He is connected with Daphne’s transformation into a laurel and, before the laurel existed, wears garlands from any tree. As father of Phaëton, he owns and drives the light-bearing chariot and its flame-footed steeds. He swears by Styx to grant Phaëton’s request, reluctantly allows him to drive, and warns him to take an oblique course; afterward he restrains the terrified steeds and reproaches them for Phaëton’s death. Through his oracle he directs Cadmus’s journey and city-founding. He discovers the intrigue of Mars and Venus, is linked to an aromatic medicinal drug, joins Diana in punishing Niobe by killing her sons, and defeats and harshly punishes Marsyas after overcoming him on the Tritonian reed.

l: Pythian games, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Pythian games are sacred contests, probably originally a religious ceremonial, named for Python and instituted by Phœbus as a memorial of Python’s death; other accounts credit Diomedes, Eurylochus the Thessalian, Amphictyon, or Adrastus. Celebrated near Delphi, they honor Apollo with a hymn accompanied by cithara. They may first have consisted only of singing, then included singing, dancing, instrumental music, boxing, running, and chariot-racing; gymnastic and equestrian exercises came later. Held every eight years before the 48th Olympiad and every four years afterward, they continued in the time of Emperor Julian. Prizes changed from beechen-leaf crowns to laurel chaplets and palm branches.

l: Daphne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Daphne is a nymph and daughter of Peneus who loves woods, hunting, and perpetual virginity, rejecting marriage, love, and suitors. Pursued by Apollo after Cupid wounds her with a leaden arrow, she flees until exhausted and seeks divine aid. She is transformed into a laurel while fleeing, retaining her former elegance.

l: Peneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Peneus is a divine river of Thessaly, flowing from the bottom of Pindus through Tempe, where it has a rocky cavern home, gives law to water Nymphs, and runs with foaming, far-heard waves, though Ælian calls its stream gentle and sluggish. Its course was probably stopped by an earthquake before Thessaly was inundated. As Daphne’s father, it urges her to marry; she seeks its aid while fleeing Apollo.

l: Inachus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Inachus is a river of Argolis, now known as Naio, and a God; accounts place its rise in Lycæus or Artemisium and name Phoroneus or Oceanus as parent. Greek authors call him Argos’s first king and Io’s father. He is said to settle in Greece as Isis worship is received, and hides in his deepest cavern, weeping for Io and swelling his waters.

l: Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Io is a nymph, daughter of Inachus and granddaughter of Phoroneus, whom Greek authors identify with Isis. After Jupiter invites her into the groves, she flees, but he overtakes and ravishes her under darkness. Jupiter changes her into a cow and entrusts her to Argus, under Juno’s control. In captivity she cannot use human speech; she tells Inachus who she is by tracing letters in dust with her foot. Juno then drives her, through Fury and invisible stings, to wander across Earth. At the Nile, the limit of her wanderings, she begs in groans, tears, and lowing for release. She regains human form, bears Epaphus through Jupiter, and is worshipped in Egypt as Isis, adored by priests and Isis’s worshippers in linen vestments. She accompanies Epaphus to Egypt; Greek accounts also say she marries Apis or Osiris.

l: Argus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Argus is a watchman, Io’s uncle, and son of Aristor or Arestor, appointed by Juno to guard Io. Described as highly vigilant and wise, he has a hundred eyes, traditionally representing his wisdom and penetration; while some sleep, others watch. He keeps Io under the greatest care from a lofty mountain, watching on all sides. He is also said to have been the fourth king of Argos after Inachus. Mercury approaches Argus with music and conversation and lulls all his eyes asleep. One account says Hierax wakes him before Mercury kills him with a stone; another says Mercury wounds, beheads, and casts his body from the rock. Argus dies, his eyes’ light is extinguished, and Juno sets the hundred eyes in a peacock’s tail.

l: Mercury, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Mercury is a god, son of Jupiter and Maia, grandson of Atlas and Pleione, born and named from Cyllene. He is Jupiter’s herald and messenger, marked by wings on his feet, a cap, mantle, caduceus, and magic wand; the caduceus summons departed souls, induces sleep, and serves heraldic offices. Ordered by Jupiter to kill Argus, he disguises himself as a shepherd, uses reeds, song, conversation, and his soporiferous wand to make Argus sleep, then kills him with a crooked sword. He steals Apollo’s cattle, tests Battus after giving him a cow to keep silent, and turns him into hard stone when he betrays the hiding place. He is filled with desire for Herse, approaches her house, and asks Aglauros for access to her apartment. After she refuses, he opens the carved door with his wand; the account says Aglauros becomes a rock through the consequences of his actions. He also begets Hermaphroditus.

l: Syrinx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Syrinx, a famous Naiad and Nymph among the Hamadryads at Nonacris, is devoted to Diana and her virginity. Dressed like Diana, she repeatedly escapes Satyrs and Gods, flees Pan, seeks Naiads’ help at the Ladon, and becomes reeds.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Juno is a goddess, daughter of Saturn, sister and wife of Jupiter, queen of Jupiter, supreme queen, and queen of the Gods. She possesses a throne and sceptre, has Iris as messenger, and her own bird is the peacock. After Argus’s death, she sets his eyes in the peacock’s tail; she is also possibly associated with Air or Æther. She is said to be the source of the Milky Way milk story. Much of Juno’s record concerns jealousy, anger, punishment, and revenge in response to Jupiter’s relationships and those connected to them. Discovering Jupiter’s intrigue, she obtains Io as a gift, gives her to Argus’s guardianship, later sends a Fury to terrify and drive Io across the earth, and finally is pacified and ends the punishment. Jealous of Calisto, she transforms her into a bear and objects when Calisto is placed among the stars. She seeks revenge on Semele by using a cloud disguise to approach her and persuading her to demand Jupiter’s full divine majesty. Juno disputes Jupiter over sexual pleasure and blinds Tiresias after his judgment. She punishes Echo by restricting her speech after Echo distracts her while Jupiter’s mistresses escape. She opposes Bacchus and sends Tisiphone against Athamas and Ino, rejoicing at the resulting violence and transforming Ino’s reproaching attendants. She persecutes the family sprung from Agenor, has hatred toward the Tyrian mistress and her race, banishes Latona and drives her to wander with her twins, and causes pestilence against Æacus’s people because their country bears a rival’s name.

l: Epaphus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Epaphus, believed born to Io from Jupiter, reigns in Egypt and has temples throughout its cities. Equal to Phaëton in spirit and years, he mocks Phaëton’s claimed parentage; according to Herodotus, he is Io’s son and identified with Apis.

l: Phaëton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phaëton is a mortal charioteer, chiefly presented as the son of the Sun, Apollo, or Phœbus and of Clymene, and as Inachus’s grandson through her. He is equal in spirit and age to Epaphus, but Epaphus’s mockery prompts him to seek proof of his divine descent. He visits the Sun’s palace and obtains permission to guide his father’s chariot for one day. Despite warnings, he drives it, loses command of the horses, and, terrified by the burning world and the Scorpion, abandons the chariot. The resulting conflagration sets the earth on fire, contributes to the darkening of the Æthiopians, and consumes his yellow hair. Jupiter kills him with lightning, and he falls headlong through the air into the Eridanus. His mother and sisters mourn him; Cycnus mourns intensely; and his father grieves, resents the disaster, and blames the flame-footed steeds. He represents rash youth that follows inclination rather than wisdom and prudence. Other accounts make him Rhoda’s son, a fourth descendant of Cecrops, or a Molossian king and student of astronomy who drowned in the Po.

l: Calisto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Calisto is a virgin of Nonacris, Lycaon’s daughter, and Diana’s most beloved Nymph, a chaste hunter armed with bow and light javelin. Jupiter seduces and assaults her, and her pregnancy is exposed among Diana’s company. Juno transforms her into a bear while she retains understanding. Unrecognized by her son Arcas, she is finally placed among the heavens by Jupiter as the Great Bear.

l: Arcas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arcas, son of Calisto and Jupiter, unknowingly nearly spears his transformed mother while hunting; Jupiter places them among the heavens as the Little Bear.

l: Coronis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Coronis is a Nymph from Larissa in Hæmonia, famed as its most beautiful woman. She pleases Apollo while chaste, becomes his mistress, then is unfaithful with a youth of Hæmonia. The bird of Phoebus reports her, and Apollo pierces her with an arrow. Dying, she laments that punishment could have waited until after childbirth, since she and her child will die together. She is transformed into a crow for her overly faithful report.

l: Æsculapius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Æsculapius is Coronis’s divine child, saved by Apollo from her womb and the flames after Apollo kills her, then carried to Chiron’s cave. Some writers say he came from a crow’s egg and was born and widely worshipped as a serpent. Foretold to become a giver of health to the whole world, he restores life to mortal bodies, though this power brings his grandsire’s bolts against him. He becomes a lifeless carcase, then a God again, renewing destiny twice. He is the tutelary divinity of Epidaurus.

l: Chiron, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Chiron is a two-formed Centaur, son of Philyra and Saturn, living in Thessaly’s mountains. Renowned for knowledge when learning was little cultivated, he is regarded as an early promulgator of medicines, an excellent musician, and a good astronomer. He teaches Æsculapius, Hercules, and Jason, marks out constellations to direct the Argonauts, and is proud of his divine pupil. Initially immortal, he is wounded in the foot by Hercules’ arrow while examining a baneful serpent; serpent blood makes him mortal. Ocyrrhoe foretells that he will wish to die, and the Gods make him subject to death.

l: Ocyrrhoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ocyrrhoë, daughter of Chiron and Chariclo, is a centaur’s daughter and prophetess trained in riding and managing horses by her father. She sings the Fates’ secrets and foretells the destinies of Æsculapius and Chiron. Prevented from speaking further, she is punished for prophetic arts by transformation into a mare and renamed Enippe.

l: Battus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Battus, an old man known in his country, keeps forests, pastures, and Neleus's mares. After witnessing Mercury's theft, he accepts payment for silence but betrays it for more, so Mercury condemns him and changes him into stone.

l: Herse, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Herse is a daughter of Cecrops and sister of Aglauros, a chaste virgin who occupies the middle bed-chamber in Cecrops’s house. Returning from Minerva’s citadel, she surpasses the other virgins in beauty, drawing Mercury’s love. Her marriage to Mercury is fortunate; she is also recorded as Cephalus’s mother. Temples of Herse and Aglauros stand at Athens.

l: Aglauros, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Aglauros, daughter of Cecrops and sister of Herse, first calls her sisters cowards and unties a basket, revealing Ericthonius with a dragon beside him; she has also seen Minerva’s hidden mysteries with a profane hand. In Cecrops’s left-hand bed-chamber, she notices Mercury seeking Herse, demands gold to assist him, and sends him away. Envy infects her, turning her jealousy of Herse’s fortune into obstinate resistance at Herse’s threshold. When Mercury opens the door, Aglauros stiffens and gradually becomes a bloodless stone statue. Temples of Herse and Aglauros later stand at Athens.

l: Agenor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Agenor is a father, identified as the son of Neptune and Libya according to Apollodorus, and husband of Telephassa. He has Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa. After Europa is ravished and carried away, he orders his sons to search for her and forbids their return without her, threatening Cadmus with exile. They fail to recover Europa and establish themselves in different countries.

l: Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Europa is a royal-born daughter of Agenor, King of Tyre, renowned for beauty and attended by Tyrian virgins. Some writers instead make her the daughter of Phœnix and Agenor’s granddaughter; her name may refer to her fair complexion. While with the virgins, she encounters Jupiter disguised as a bull, overcomes her fear, touches and decorates him, and sits on his back. Jupiter carries her across the sea to Crete. Agenor then sends Cadmus to seek and return her. After her death, Europa is honored as a divinity and called Hellotis.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cadmus is a son of Agenor, brother of Europa, Sidonian stranger, exile, and founder and long-time ruler of Thebes. Sent from Phœnicia under the demand that he find Europa, he wanders in search of her and cannot recover her. After living in Thrace until his mother Telephassa dies, he goes to Delphi and consults the oracle of Phœbus. Obeying its direction, he follows an unyoked heifer to its resting place, prepares a sacrifice to Jupiter, and sends servants for water. When his companions are destroyed by a dragon, he kills it with his spear. On Minerva's advice he sows its teeth; earth-born armed warriors arise, destroy one another, and the five survivors help him build Thebes and its walls. He settles in Bœotia and, according to one account, serves Mars for a year to expiate killing the dragon. He later prospers through his wife Hermione, children, and grandchildren, though calamities begin with Actæon's death. He is father of Semele, Ino, and Agave, and is said to have caused Semele and her son to be thrown into the sea. After many woes, sorrow, prodigies, and a conspiracy that drives him from Thebes, he retires or is exiled with Hermione to Illyria. There he commands an army, is chosen king, assists the Enchelians, and receives the crown of Illyria. In old age he recalls the dragon, wishes to become a serpent, and transforms: scales cover his skin, his body becomes black with azure spots, his tongue divides and hisses, though his arms remain. Other accounts describe him as leading a colony into Greece, establishing Europe, building Nygnis, bringing cuirasses and brazen darts, or as an officer of Agenor who eloped with a singing girl.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Thebes is a Bœotian city, named under a stated theory from the Greek word βοῦς, founded and built by Cadmus where a heifer lay down as Phœbus instructed. With the five surviving earth-born warriors produced from the dragon’s teeth, Cadmus builds its walls and a citadel to secure a fortified settlement; the city stands during his prosperity and is inhabited by Theban people. Its history is marked by the fates of Actæon, Semele, Pentheus, and Niobe. Cadmus is driven from the throne and Pentheus rules, fearing capture by Bacchus; after Pentheus’s death, the Ismenian matrons adopt the new worship. Thebes suffers famine during the conflict involving Ino and Athamas, then Cadmus leaves because of his family’s misfortunes and prodigies. Under Niobe and Amphion, its women are told to worship Latona and her children, but Apollo and Diana destroy Niobe’s children at Cadmus’s citadel. A plague also ravages the city.

l: Actæon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Actæon is a skilled hunter, grandson of Cadmus and son of Autonoë and Aristæus, brought up by Chiron and owner of a large hunting pack. After postponing the rest of a hunt, he enters the Gargaphie grove and accidentally sees Diana bathing. Diana punishes him by transforming him into a stag. His own dogs pursue and tear him to pieces, and he dies, said to be killed on Mount Cithæron.

l: Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Semele is a mortal female, daughter of Cadmus, and Jupiter’s lover. Pregnant by Jupiter with Bacchus, she accepts Juno’s deceptive advice, given while disguised as Beroë, and asks Jupiter to appear as he is received by Juno. When Jupiter visits as promised, his lightning overwhelms her mortal body; she burns to ashes among her nuptial presents while pregnant. She is Bacchus’s mother, with one account saying she delivered him in the seventh month and Jupiter carried him for the remaining period. She is buried at Oreate. After death she is ranked among the Goddesses as Thyone, is brought from hell to heaven by Bacchus, and there converses and eats with gods.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus is a god and deity, also called Liber, whose central account begins with Semele: he is her son, survives her destruction while she is pregnant, and undergoes a premature birth from her womb into Jupiter’s thigh, with Jupiter undertaking a mother’s duties during gestation. Ino secretly nurses and fosters him, and the Nyseian Nymphs conceal and nourish him in caves at Nysa, away from Juno’s fury. The cave’s two entrances give him the name Dithyrites, and Nysa contributes to the Greek name Dionysus. He later goes down to hell, brings Semele out, and carries her to heaven. The records also preserve several differing genealogies and identities: he is said to be Semele and Jupiter’s son in the Theban account, while Cicero’s account distinguishes five Bacchuses, respectively sons of Proserpina and Jupiter, the Nile, Caprius, Moon and Jupiter, and Nisus and Thione. One of these founds Nysa; another tradition reasonably identifies Bacchus with Osiris. Bacchus arrives in Greece in triumph as a new god. Associated with vine cultivation, useful arts, thyrsi, tambourines, ivy, wine, and ecstatic worship, he teaches and civilizes, spreads his rites, and is worshipped through Bacchic rites, the Dionysia, and a triennial nocturnal festival. Festive cries, Bacchanals, Satyrs, and drunken Silenus follow him; he rides lynxes yoked to his chariot. He is eternally youthful, conquers the East as far as India and the Ganges, is worshipped in India, and is honored with temples in Achaia. His power is also punitive. When sailors deceive him, he arrests their ship, produces vines and wild creatures, changes the crew into dolphin-like creatures, and spares Acœtes. He destroys or punishes Pentheus and Lycurgus, and punishes the daughters of Minyas for contempt of his worship and desecration of his festival, transforming them into bats and their webs into vines. His names include Bromius, Lyæus, Thyoneus, Lenæus, Nyctelius, Eleleus, Iacchus, and Evan, each linked to worship, wine, Semele, frenzy, night, or cries. His power is celebrated in Thebes, where Ino invokes him while fleeing with Melicerta. Other recorded acts include seeking rejuvenation for his nurses and hiding a stolen bullock as a fictitious stag.

l: Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Tiresias is a prophet and renowned soothsayer, son of Evenus and Chariclo, who has lived as both man and woman. After striking coupling serpents, he becomes a woman for seven autumns; striking them again in the eighth year restores his former sex and shape. Having known both male and female pleasure, he judges Jupiter and Juno’s dispute over sexual pleasure in Jupiter’s favor. Juno blinds him, and Jupiter compensates him with prophecy and prophetic knowledge. He gives unerring answers to those who consult him, is praised throughout Achaia, and predicts Narcissus’s fate and Pentheus’s violent death if Pentheus will not honor Bacchus, though Pentheus mocks his blindness. He lives to great age and is blind in old age. Other accounts attribute his blindness to Minerva after he sees her bathing, connect it with writings or teachings about sexual differences, and say he dies after drinking from the fountain of Telphusa when overheated.

l: Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Narcissus is a beautiful youth, a Thespian by birth and son of Cephisus and Liriope, celebrated throughout Aonia but marked by stubborn pride. Many youths and damsels court him, and Echo follows him through forests, yet he despises and rejects suitors, Nymphs, youths, and Echo’s embrace. After hunting, he reaches a clear spring and falls in love with his own reflection, mistaking it for a body. He neglects food and rest, pines away, bids farewell to the image, and dies. Received into the infernal abodes, he still looks at himself in the Stygian waters. He is transformed into a flower whose fading duration reflects his career; his name is said to derive from ναρκᾷν, “to fade away.”

l: Echo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Echo is a noisy Nymph, also described by poets as daughter of the Air and the Tongue. She distracted Juno with stories so Jupiter’s mistresses could escape, and Juno punished her to repeat only others’ last words. After seeing Narcissus in the forest, Echo loved him, but his rejection drove her to hide, waste away, and transform into sound; only Echo’s voice survived. She still echoes Narcissus’s cries and final words, grieving him despite anger over his treatment of her.

l: Pentheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pentheus is the son of Echion and Agave, grandson of Cadmus, and king of Thebes after Cadmus. He is described as a contemner of the gods who refuses to honor Bacchus, ridicules Tiresias, forbids Bacchic rites, and orders Bacchus captured. Seeking to suppress or punish the Bacchantes and their mysteries, he goes to Mount Cithæron, in one account climbing a tree to observe secret rites. Discovered there, he is attacked and torn apart by Agave and the other Bacchantes.

l: Alcithoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Alcithoë, daughter of Minyas and sister of Aristippe/Arsinoë and Leucippe, rejects Bacchus’s festival and rites, denying his parentage, alongside her sisters. While weaving at a hanging web after her sisters fall silent, she takes up the telling of transformations to entertain her listeners; she is associated with the daughters of Minyas being changed into bats.

l: Pyramus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pyramus is the most beautiful youth and Thisbe’s lover. In a tale of youthful love and parental resentment, he meets her near Ninus’s tomb in Babylon; believing she has been killed, he mourns, wounds himself with his sword, and dies beneath their agreed-upon tree.

l: Thisbe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Thisbe is a maiden and Pyramus’s beloved, favored among the damsels of the East. She reaches their meeting place first, flees from a lioness, returns to find Pyramus dead by his own hand, and kills herself; their story warns youth and parents.

l: Mars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: An ennobled deity also called Mavors, Mars sets a dragon to watch a spot and neighboring stream and, in one interpretation, fathers it. Mars is Venus’s gallant and Hermione’s parent with Venus; the Sun discovers their adultery, and Vulcan catches them embracing. Cadmus serves Mars for killing the dragon.

l: Venus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Venus is a goddess and ennobled deity associated with the sea and foam, said to have risen from the sea and landed at Cythera; she is also called Erycina. Wife of Vulcan and mother of Cupid, she commits adultery with Mars, is exposed by the Sun, and seeks revenge by making the Sun feel similar passion. She pities Ino and Melicerta after they enter the sea, asking Neptune to admit them among the sea deities. Through Cupid, she seeks to extend her and her son’s sway over Tartarus by having him strike Pluto. She is also linked to Hermione, Ino, and a transformation into a fish while fleeing the Giants.

l: Leucothoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Leucothoë is chiefly a maiden and Nymph, daughter of Eurynome and Orchamus, who grows more beautiful than her mother and is attended by twelve handmaids. The Sun, captivated by her, approaches disguised as Eurynome, reveals himself, and embraces her. After Clytie reveals the affair, Orchamus buries her alive; the grieving Sun transforms her body into a frankincense tree. An explanatory account connects her with Persia, while another identifies Leucothoë as Ino’s new sea-deity name after Neptune transforms her.

l: Clytie, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Clytie, a nymph and Leucothoë’s rival, passionately loves the Sun and envies Leucothoë for his love. She reveals Leucothoë’s affair to her father; when the Sun rejects her, she fasts nine days and watches his path across the sky. Rooted in the ground, she is transformed into a sunflower while retaining her passion.

l: Salmacis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Salmacis is a Naiad nymph who dwells at a pool, avoids hunting and archery, and bathes, arranges her hair, rests, and gathers flowers. After seeing Hermaphroditus, she loves and pursues him despite his resistance, clinging to him in water until their bodies are united.

l: Hermaphroditus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Hermaphroditus, son of Mercury and the Cytherean Goddess and nursed by Naiads in Ida’s caves, bears both parents’ features and is named for them. He rejects Salmacis, but her seizure in a spring unites them. The fountain transforms him from male into a two-shaped, half-male youth; he asks his parents to impose this change on men entering it.

l: Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ino, daughter of Cadmus and sister of Semele, becomes Athamas’s wife after Nephele and bears Learchus and Melicerta. She opposes Nephele’s children, orders their sacrifice, and, according to the myth, causes the famine at Thebes. Poisoned by Tisiphone and driven mad, she flees after Athamas kills Learchus, carrying Melicerta. She calls on Bacchus, leaps into the sea, and Neptune transforms her into Leucothoë, later called Matuta at Rome.

l: Melicerta, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Melicerta, son of Ino and Athamas, flees Athamas carried by Ino and leaps with her into the sea. Neptune removes his mortality, transforming him into Palæmon, a sea deity worshipped in Greece and Rome as Palæmon and by Romans as Portunus.

l: Illyria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Illyria is the coast where exiled Cadmus and Hermione arrive after wandering, retire from Thebes, and where Cadmus commands its army, becomes king, and dies.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Perseus is a hero, youth, son of Danaë and Jupiter or Jove, grandson of Acrisius, and, in the stated descent, descended from Danaë. He is associated with Danaë’s removal to Seriphus and with Polydectes’ care of his education; later, required to bring Polydectes Medusa’s head, he undertakes many toils. Using a reflecting shield associated with Minerva, Talaria, and a Cyllenian falchion, he kills Medusa without being seen, takes her head, and escapes the pursuing Gorgon sisters. The head becomes both proof of his victory and a weapon, though its power to turn enemies to stone is also interpreted as a metaphor for his heroism and the terror of his victory. Carrying it, he travels over Africa and throughout the world. When Atlas refuses hospitality and threatens him, Perseus exposes the head and turns Atlas into a mountain; he also lays it on sea plants beneath the sea, changing sea-weed into coral. In Æthiopia, he kills the sea monster threatening Andromeda, rescues and marries her. At their wedding, attacked by Phineus and his followers, he fights until he uses the head to petrify Phineus. He later enters his native city with Andromeda, attacks Prœtus in defense and vengeance for Danaë, and returns victorious to Polydectes, turning him to stone after finding Danaë and Dictys at the altars of the Deities. Records also credit him with recovering the Golden Fleece and include differing interpretations of him as a fugitive from Argos or an enemy of Andromeda.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Medusa is a viperous monster and Gorgon, daughter of Phorcys, described in some accounts as a ruler, one of three wealthy sisters, or a beautiful woman. She is deflowered by Poseidon in the Temple of Minerva and has serpents mingled with her hair. Her petrifying gaze turns beholders, men, and beasts to stone. Perseus approaches her through her reflection in a shield while she sleeps, seizes her by the hair, and beheads her. Her blood produces Pegasus and Chrysaor, and drops from her carried head produce serpents. Perseus carries and uses her head as a weapon and proof of her death; its face turns Polydectes to stone without blood.

l: Atlas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Atlas, son of Iapetus and king of his country, is vast, supports Heaven, and owns a walled orchard with golden fruit guarded by a dragon. Father of Maia and grandfather of messenger, he rejects and expels Perseus because of an oracle; Perseus shows Medusa’s head, transforming Atlas into a mountain.

l: Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and Cassiope, is bound by her arms to a rock and exposed to a sea monster to be devoured, as punishment for her mother’s boast about beauty. Though betrothed to Phineus, she is rescued from sacrifice by Perseus, liberated after he turns Atlas into a mountain. After sea-weed is changed into coral, she marries Perseus and enters his native city with him. She is central to a story associated with Æthiopia or the coast of Africa near Joppa, where chain marks reportedly remained on a rock.

l: Phineus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phineus, brother of Cepheus, king of Bithynia, and Andromeda’s uncle and former betrothed, is described as most righteous. Angered when Andromeda is given to Perseus, he leads an attack, then surrenders after his followers are petrified. Perseus petrifies him with the Gorgon head, fixing his fearful, supplicant expression.

l: Polydectes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Polydectes is the ruler and king of Seriphus, brother of Dictys. While preparing to marry Hippodamia, he loves Danaë and violently threatens Danaë and Dictys. He hates Perseus, dismisses Perseus’s victory over Medusa, and demands Medusa’s head. When Perseus returns, he uses Medusa’s face to transform Polydectes into stone.

l: Helicon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Helicon, produced by Pegasus's hoof, is the Muses' habitation amid sacred streams, groves, caves, and flower-covered grass, visited by Minerva.

l: Muses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Muses are virgin Mnemonian maids, sisters of Urania and daughters of Jupiter and Mnemosyne, also called Aonides and Mnemonides. They inhabit Mount Helicon, a sacred retreat associated with the fountain made by Pegasus’s hoof. They welcome Minerva, recount Pyreneus’s threat and the Pierides’ challenge, and are declared by the Nymphs to have defeated the Emathian sisters in song.

l: Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pyreneus is a dreadful, insolent prince and unjust ruler of Daulian and Phocean land in Phocis, backed by Thracian troops. Hostile to learning, he destroyed institutions of instruction. During a storm he invited the Muses into his house and attempted violence; they escaped by taking wing, and he lost his life.

l: Pierides, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Pierides are nine sisters, daughters of Pierus and Evippe. They challenge the Muses in a contest of voice and skill, are defeated, and become magpies, increasing the number of birds; the change symbolizes poor, empty stories associated with Pierus’s works.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine, also called Pherephata, is a goddess of childlike innocence, a virgin if permitted to remain so, and chiefly the daughter and only daughter of Ceres, though one report calls her daughter of Erectheus. Inclined toward virginity, she gathers violets and white lilies with companions near Pergus. Pluto sees her and violently abducts her; she cries for Ceres and her companions as her flowers fall. In the world of darkness she is sad but becomes Pluto’s powerful spouse, wife, and queen of the shades. Having eaten seven pomegranate grains, she is subject to the Destinies’ law and cannot return completely to the upper world. She becomes a common divinity of two kingdoms, spending equal months with Ceres and Pluto. Her sacred flower is the Narcissus flower, and she changes Ascalaphus into an owl.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres is an ennobled, genial, fertile goddess of corn and agriculture, credited as the first to turn the earth with the crooked plough, give corn and wholesome food, and establish laws; agriculture and civilization are described as her gifts. Her worship is highly esteemed at Henna, and her mysteries are established at Eleusis. She is the mother of Proserpina, also called Proserpine and her only daughter. When her daughter disappears and Pluto carries her away, Ceres searches all lands, seas, and the whole world without rest, using pine torches lit at Ætna and drinking barley liquor when thirsty. She learns from Arethusa that her daughter is in the world of darkness, grieves and angers, damages Sicily's agriculture, and appeals to Jupiter. Jupiter's decision governs Proserpine's periods on earth and in the Infernal Regions; Ceres accepts it and rejoices at recovering her. Ceres also sends Triptolemus in her dragon-drawn chariot to scatter seed and cultivate the earth, having nursed him with her milk and purified him by fire. When Lyncus tries to kill him, she transforms Lyncus into a lynx.

l: Cyane, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cyane is a celebrated Sicilian Nymph, guardian and namesake of her pool, wife of Anapis, and companion of Proserpine. She rises to oppose Pluto's seizure of Proserpina, but after he forces through her stream, grief dissolves her into its waters.

l: Ascalaphus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus, son of Orphne and Acheron and a courtier of Pluto, advises Pluto to carry away Proserpine. After seeing Proserpine eat seven pomegranate grains, he reveals it, obstructing her restoration to Ceres. Ceres or Proserpine punishes him; accounts make him a rock, an owl with great eyes, or a lizard.

l: Sirens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sirens are daughters of Acheloüs and one of the Muses. Seeking Proserpine throughout the world, they ask the Gods to transform them into birds; afterward they have feathers and bird feet while retaining maiden faces and human voices.

l: Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arethusa is a nymph of the Alpheian waters and of Achaia, native to Pisa and born from Elis, later a sacred spring, river, and fountain on Ortygia in Sicily. A robust, beautiful hunter and Diana’s protected armor-bearer, she hunted through glades and set nets. While bathing, she was pursued by Alpheus; Diana hid her in a cloud, after which she became a stream. Carried beneath spacious seas and through Earth’s lowest caverns, she flowed through Styx, saw Proserpine as queen and spouse of the Infernal King, and told Ceres of her fate. She finally reached Ortygia’s upper air, where she has her abode as a fountain.

l: Lyncus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Lyncus, king of Scythia, hosts Triptolemus, then envies and tries to kill him; for this cruelty, Ceres transforms him into a lynx.

l: Triptolemus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Triptolemus is a youth from Athens, priest of Ceres, and ruler at Eleusis when her mysteries were established. He carries Ceres’s seeds and corn to spread fruitful harvests, wholesome food, and her worship across different countries. He travels by ship and through the sky in Ceres’s chariot, associated with winged dragons, over Europe, Asia, and the earth; in Scythia he tells Lyncus that he comes to provide food. Traditions also say Ceres nursed and purified him.

l: Arachne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arachne is a Lydian weaver and artist, daughter of Idmon and her mother, from humble Hypaepa and low extraction. Renowned throughout Lydia for exceptional skill in working wool, silk, and weaving, she is also said to have invented making linen cloths and nets. She challenges Minerva, or Pallas, to a weaving contest and creates a web representing transformations, deceptions, and numerous myths of the gods. After Minerva strikes her, Arachne hangs herself in despair. Minerva then takes pity on her and transforms her into a spider, completing the transformation associated with her challenge and web.

l: Niobe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Niobe is a daughter of Tantalus, sister of Pelops, wife of Amphion, and queen of Thebes, also described as descended from Atlas. She possesses immense wealth and takes particular pride in her lineage, beauty, and children, whose number is variously given as twelve, fourteen, or twenty. During worship of Latona, Niobe claims superiority over her and contemptuously orders Theban women to abandon Latona’s sacrifice. Apollo and Diana then slay all her sons and daughters, and Amphion dies. Bereft of her family, Niobe retires to Mount Sipylus in Lydia, is borne to a mountain by a whirlwind, and hardens into a statue, rock, or stone that continues to shed tears.

l: Latona, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Latona is a goddess and Titaness, daughter of Cæus and mother of Apollo and Diana, her twins. Banished by Juno, she wanders with her children, is received by floating Delos, and leans against a palm during their birth. Honored by Theban women, she is mocked by Niobe, whose insult prompts Apollo and Diana to avenge her. Later, exhausted and thirsty in Lycia, Latona seeks water to bathe her children; after countrymen refuse, insult her, and muddy the water, she curses them to remain in the pool, later changing them into frogs, then travels toward Xanthus.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Diana is a Delian, Ortygian goddess of the woods, hunt, bow and arrows, associated with the Moon and perhaps identified with Isis. She is Phoebe, sister of the Sun and Apollo, daughter of Latona, and a perpetual virgin attended by Nymphs. Accounts also distinguish three Dianas, naming daughters of Jupiter and Proserpine, Jupiter and Latona, and Upis and Glauce; one episode is probably attributed to Diana Britomartis, who is especially fond of hunting. Chaste and prudent in explanation yet severe in action, she joins Apollo in punishing Niobe’s daughters after Latona’s complaint, hides Arethusa in a cloud and carries her to Ortygia, expels Calisto when her pregnancy reveals a broken vow, and punishes Actæon for seeing her bathe at Gargaphie by turning him into a stag. She is incensed at Œneus for omitting her first-fruit offering and is believed subject to magicians during an eclipse.

l: Marsyas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Marsyas is a satyr and musician, chiefly identified as Hyagnis’s son, though Hyginus names Œagrius as his father. He learns the flute from Hyagnis and becomes skilled enough to challenge Apollo in a trial of musical skill. Apollo overcomes him on the Tritonian reed and punishes his presumption by having him flayed alive. His body is delivered to Olympus for burial; one account instead says that, ashamed by defeat, he throws himself into the river later bearing his name.

l: Pelops, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pelops, brother of Amphion's mother, alone mourns and reveals the ivory on his left shoulder by drawing his clothes aside.

l: Tereus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Tereus is a Thracian, Odrysian king, descended from Gradivus, powerful in wealth and men. He marries Progne and fathers Itys. After conquering barbarous troops at Athens, he travels there to bring Philomela to Thrace, lusts after her, rapes her, cuts out her tongue, and hides her in a remote dwelling, then falsely reports her death to Progne. Progne later serves him Itys’s remains at a banquet. Learning this, Tereus pursues Progne and Philomela with a sword, but is transformed into an epops, or lapwing, whose association with filth and impurity symbolizes his character.

l: Progne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Progne is the daughter of Pandion, sister of Philomela, wife of Tereus, mother of Itys, and a queen. She first asks Tereus to bring Philomela from Athens, then mourns when she believes his false report that Philomela is dead. Philomela’s woven message reveals Tereus’s crimes, driving Progne to revenge. During a nocturnal Bacchic procession, she uses Bacchus’s rites as a disguise to rescue Philomela from captivity. She and Philomela murder Itys and serve his remains to Tereus. Fleeing Tereus, Progne is transformed into a swallow, associated with restless searching for her son.

l: Philomela, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Philomela is a daughter of Pandion and sister of Progne, described as a Cecropian or Athenian Nymph. Wanting to visit Progne, she is taken by Tereus to Thrace, where he rapes her, cuts out her tongue, and imprisons her in an ancient wood. Unable to speak, she reveals his crime to Progne through a woven message. Rescued and brought to Tereus's house, she helps Progne murder Itys and throws Itys's bloody head at Tereus. After his pursuit, Philomela is transformed into a nightingale; other accounts call her a swallow. Her bird form’s hiding in woods and thickets represents her concealed misfortunes and sorrows.

l: Pandion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pandion, king of Athens and father of Progne and Philomela, entrusts Philomela to Tereus, urges her swift return, and dies in Tartarus before old age.

l: Erectheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Erectheus is king of Athens, receiving its sceptre and government. He sends for corn from Egypt during famine, fathers Orithyïa among eight children, and refuses Boreas’s marriage to her. Told he will win by sacrificing daughter Proserpine, he wars with Eleusinians and is killed alongside Eumolpus. Accounts differ on his relation to Pandion.

l: Boreas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Boreas is a winged god and north wind, also called Aquilo, governing northern regions and king of Thrace. After Erectheus refuses his marriage suit to Orithyïa, he uses his winds to carry her by force from near the Ilissus to Ciconian lands; they become spouses and parents of Calaïs and Zethes.

l: Zethes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Zethes, twin son of Boreas and Orithyïa, begins without feathers, later grows wings like his father’s, reaches youth, and joins Jason and the Minyæ in the search for the Golden Fleece.

l: Argonauts, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Argonauts, also called the Minyæ, are young Greek nobles and adventurers who sail the Pagasæan ship Argo with Jason. After visiting Lemnos, taking wives, and rescuing Phineus from the Harpies, they reach Colchis, witness Jason’s success, and celebrate his victory.

l: Jason, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jason is a hero, native of Iolcos, son of Æson, and leader of the Argonauts. He leads an expedition to Colchis to seek the Golden Fleece. There he asks Æetes for it and, aided by Medea, survives the imposed labors: he conquers the fire-breathing, brazen-footed bulls, makes them plough, sows the serpent’s teeth, and causes the armed Earth-born warriors to destroy one another. Medea also helps him put the fleece’s dragon to sleep, enabling him to obtain the Golden Fleece and depart with Medea and his companions. He returns victoriously to Iolcos and marries Medea, as promised for her help. He later asks Medea to rejuvenate his aged father Æson, reconciles with Pelias and Pelias’s children, and gives the crown to Acastus. After becoming tired of Medea, he marries Glauce, Creon’s daughter, while Medea is away, and witnesses Medea murder their two children.

l: Medea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Medea is a royal maiden of Colchis, daughter of Æetes and, according to some writers, Hecate’s daughter; she is renowned as an enchantress and sorceress skilled in herbs, potions, rites, and potent magic. Aided by Juno through Venus, she falls violently in love with Jason while divided between that love and loyalty to her father and homeland. She agrees to assist his expedition if he marries her, gives him enchanted herbs and protective charms against the bulls, warriors, and dragon, helps him reach the palace and take its treasures, then betrays her family and country by fleeing with him to Greece as his wife. She restores Jason’s father Æson to youth through elaborate rites, herbs, sacrifices, and a potion. She next takes revenge on Pelias by deceiving his daughters into attacking him and completes his death through the cauldron. Afterward she goes to Corinth. When Jason marries Glauce, or Creüsa, daughter of King Creon, Medea burns the palace, kills her two sons by Jason, and evades punishment by flying away in a heavenly, winged chariot drawn by dragons. Later she marries Ægeus in Athens and seeks succession for her son Medus. She prepares a poisoned cup from Scythian wolfsbane for Theseus, but when Ægeus prevents him from drinking it, she escapes amid clouds raised by enchantments.

l: Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Golden Fleece is a fictional treasure: a fleece of Phryxus, glittering with shining golden hair, and the prize sought in Colchis. Calaïs and Zethes seek it with the Minyæ, while Jason seeks it from Æetes. Guarded by a dragon, it is taken after the dragon is lulled to sleep; Jason, aided by Medea after conquering fire-breathing bulls and producing armed men from serpent’s teeth, carries it away. It is later recovered by the Argonauts. Notes present it as poetic and suggest links to treasure or Phryxus’s gilt sheep skin.

l: Æson, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Æson is Jason’s father, decrepit, aged, and near death. When Jason seeks help, Medea puts him into deep sleep, cuts his throat, and replaces his old blood with magical juices. Her magic or potion restores his hair, vigor, blood, youthful appearance, spirits, and strength, returning him to youth.

l: Pelias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pelias, Æson’s brother, dethrones him and usurps his kingdom, becoming king and father of daughters. Warned by an oracle to fear a one-shoed person, he tries to send Æson’s son Jason on a dangerous expedition. In old age, he is deceived by Medea: his daughters, hoping to restore his youth, stab him; Medea cuts his throat and puts him in a boiling cauldron.

l: Ægeus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ægeus is king and ruler of Athens, brother of Pallas, father of Theseus, and husband of Medea. Jealous of Androgeus and aware that Pallas’s sons conspire against him, he causes Androgeus’s assassination. After sheltering and marrying Medea, he unknowingly offers Theseus a poisoned cup, recognizes him by his sword’s hilt, and saves him. He then celebrates Theseus with sacrifices, gifts, and a festival, later receiving help against Minos.

l: Theseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Theseus, son of Ægeus, comes to Athens after winning peace in the Isthmus by valor. Medea tries to destroy him with aconite, but Ægeus recognizes him through the marked ivory-hilted sword and shoes Theseus took from beneath a stone, and saves him. The people celebrate his deeds: he slew the bull at Marathon, killed the Cromyon boar, defeated violent robbers, overcame dangers around Attica and neighboring regions, and killed Pallas with Pallas’s sons.

l: Minos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Minos is a king of Crete, probably the second prince of that name, son and successor of Lycastus, ruler of a hundred cities. Before the war, he conquers several islands adjoining Crete, gains control of the seas, and possesses notable strength in soldiers and shipping. After his son Androgeus dies, Minos sends for auxiliaries, seeks revenge, and prepares war against Athens and its allies. He crosses the sea with a swift, strong fleet, securing support through treaty or conquest, and seeks Æacus’s alliance. Æacus refuses because of a compact with the people of Cecropia; Minos leaves sadly, choosing threats of war over an early attack on the island. He wages war against Ægeus and leads his fleet against Ægina. Later, after Procris flees to his court, he loves her and gives her a dog.

l: Æacus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Æacus is a king of Œnopia and Ægina, grandson of Asopus, son of Ægina and Jupiter, and father of Telamon, Peleus, and Phocus. He rules a kingdom of a hundred cities whose numerous inhabitants are devastated by a pestilence. Allied with Athens, he refuses Minos’s request, welcomes Cephalus, and grants Athens military assistance. Grieving for his lost people, he asks Jupiter either to restore them or bury him with them. After seeing ants, he requests citizens as numerous as they are; when they become men, he recognizes them, gives them the empty city and lands, and names them Myrmidons. Another account says he brought industrious people from Thessaly to repopulate the island.

l: Myrmidons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Myrmidons are a race or group named from the Greek word for ants. In one account, severe pestilence leads to ants being transformed into men; in another, they are surviving subjects of Æacus, or a barbarous, industrious people of Thessaly brought by Æacus to his island. They are thrifty, patient of toil, tenacious in acquiring and storing goods, and receive Æacus’s city and lands. When the East wind turns south, they attend war with equal years and courage.

l: Cephalus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cephalus is the son of Deïoneus and Diomeda, grandson of Æolus, prince, hunter, and later an ambassador from Athens. He marries Procris, and their early life is loving and happy. According to Ovid and other writers, Aurora carries him off; he later returns to Procris, though he is also said to love Aurora. Hunting and the chase shape his life: he frequents the forest, owns Lælaps, and uses a javelin. His affectionate calls to the breeze lead Procris to suspect him; he then tests her in disguise, later admits his fault, and they reconcile. When Procris hides in a thicket, he mistakes her sound for a wild beast and kills her with his javelin, leaving him grief-stricken and condemned to perpetual banishment in Cephalenia. As Athens’s ambassador, carrying an olive branch, he invokes old alliances and helps obtain Æacus’s forces for Athens.

l: Phocus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phocus, Æacus’s son and a Nereian youth, receives Cephalus and the sons of Pallas while Telamon and his brother levy men for war. He notices Cephalus’s javelin, asks its origin and powers, and listens to Cephalus’s account.

l: Aurora, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Aurora is a goddess dwelling in the eastern quarter, opening purple doors in the ruddy east at dawn and possessing the Sun's chariot. She becomes enamoured of Cephalus while he hunts and carries him away against his will. When he rejects her for Procris, she angrily returns him, alters his appearance to test Procris, and fosters his suspicions of her fidelity.

l: Procris, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Procris is the daughter of Erectheus, king of Athens, sister of Orithyïa, and wife of Cephalus. She loves Cephalus until death, though their marriage is marked by separation, disguise, jealousy, and reconciliation. When the disguised Cephalus tests her, she resists him as faithful to her absent husband, then flees in shame after recognizing him; he seeks forgiveness, and they reconcile. In accounts mentioning Pteleon, she has an amour with him, a report of her infidelity follows, and she flees to Minos’s court in Crete. She later lives at Thoricus, returns to Cephalus, and gives him Lælaps and a celebrated javelin. Believing he loves the Nymph Aura, she hides in a forest to watch him and is fatally wounded in the breast by the javelin, asking him not to share their marriage with Aura.

l: Lælaps, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Lælaps is a dog given by Procris to Cephalus after their reconciliation, originally a celebrated gift said to have been made by Vulcan and passed through several owners. It surpasses other dogs in running and cannot be outpaced by any wild beast. Freed during a hunt, it pursues the beast with extraordinary speed until both are transformed into stone.

l: javelin, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Javelin is a beautiful weapon of unknown wood with a golden point. Given by Cynthia to Procris and then by Procris to Cephalus, it always strikes what it is aimed at, cannot be escaped, and returns to its thrower bloodstained without retrieval. During a hunt, Cephalus throws it at what he believes is a wild beast; it strikes and kills Procris, marking their reconciliation.

l: Phaëton’s conflagration, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The conflagration of the earth is associated with the flames caused by Phaëton’s fall, which intensify the fires of Ætna and ravage countries. It is also linked to the possibility that the story arose from a historical episode of heavenly flames or excessive heat.

l: Jason’s recovery of the Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_achieved_with_aid_of Medea Jason’s recovery of the Golden Fleece depends on Medea’s aid. He conquers the fire-breathing bulls, sows the serpent’s teeth, and lulls the dragon to sleep before obtaining it.

l: David McKay edition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A 1899 Philadelphia two-volume David McKay reprint, with an introduction by Edward Brooks, underlies the e-text. It begins with front matter, corrects some George Bell errors, but introduces others and uses American spelling and altered punctuation.

l: Athens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Athens is a city and kingdom, sacred to Minerva, also called Tritonian, and traditionally named for her after her dispute with Neptune over its patronage. Its prosperity is linked to Minerva, the olive tree, and agricultural pursuits, with the Senate or Areiopagus deciding the contest. After the inundation, Deucalion is said to have built a temple to Jupiter and instituted sacrifices there, under Cranaus or Cecrops; Cecrops ruled Athens. Ericthonius and Amphictyon disputed its crown, and Ericthonius instituted the Panathenæa. Erectheus ruled during conflict with the Eleusinians, after which his descendants received the kingship. At Athens, Ægeus recognizes Theseus and saves him from Medea; he also has Androgeus murdered near Œnoë after the Panathenæa, leading Minos toward war. Athens then sends Cephalus to Æacus, who grants aid.

l: Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sicily, also called Trinacria for its three corners or promontories, is a vast island and land faithful to Ceres. Heaped upon Typhœus’s limbs, it keeps him beneath its heavy mass. It is the setting of Ceres’s rule and Proserpine’s carrying away: Ceres finds evidence of her loss there, breaks ploughs, kills husbandmen and oxen, and makes fertility fail. It contains Arethusa’s Alpheian waters and was settled by Phoenicians before Greeks visited.

l: poetry, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Poetry was Ovid’s natural inclination and lasting vocation, although his father initially discouraged him from pursuing it. Ovid eventually abandoned law and public life for poetry, gained distinguished friends and admirers, and wrote works including the Metamorphoses.

l: Augustus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Augustus is an emperor and ruler addressed by Ovid. His subjects are affectionately devoted to him, in concern likened to the Gods’ regard for Jupiter. Displeased around 8 A.D. by an allegedly immoral composition, he orders Ovid from Rome to Tomi, possibly amid scandals involving Julia and his granddaughter.

l: Tomi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_on Euxine Sea [on its shore] Tomi was a colony on the shore of the Euxine sea to which Augustus ordered Ovid to withdraw. Ovid lived there in banishment until his death in 18 A.D.

l: Ovid's exile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: takes_place_in Tomi [on the shore of the Euxine Sea] Ovid’s exile began when Augustus ordered him to leave Rome for Tomi around 8 A.D. Its exact cause remained unclear, though it was probably connected to an objectionable composition and scandals involving members of Augustus’s family. Ovid never returned to Rome and died in banishment at Tomi.
